SME360.name: SME360 Free Business Health Assessment
SME360.audience: micro and small businesses, SMEs, startups, traders, manufacturers and service providers

questions.text: Does your business have clearly defined goals?

options.A: Yes, with measurable targets.
options.B: Yes, but the goals are not measurable.
options.C: We have general ideas about what we want to achieve.
options.D: We have no clearly defined business goals.

questions.text: Do you have a documented business plan or action plan?

options.A: Yes, and we review it regularly.
options.B: Yes, but we rarely review it.
options.C: We have an informal plan.
options.D: We do not have a business plan or action plan.

questions.text: How do you make important business decisions?

options.A: Using business records, market information and analysis.
options.B: Using some information alongside experience.
options.C: Mainly using experience and intuition.
options.D: Without a consistent decision-making process.

questions.text: How regularly do you review your business performance?

options.A: Monthly or more frequently, using records and targets.
options.B: Every few months.
options.C: Occasionally, when problems arise.
options.D: We do not regularly review performance.

questions.text: How consistently do you record business income and expenses?

options.A: Consistently, with organised records.
options.B: Most of the time, but some transactions are missed.
options.C: Occasionally, without a consistent system.
options.D: We do not maintain proper records.

questions.text: Do you regularly separate personal money from business money?

options.A: Yes, completely.
options.B: Mostly, with occasional mixing.
options.C: We separate them sometimes.
options.D: We regularly mix personal and business money.

questions.text: How well do you understand your business's profitability?

options.A: We regularly calculate revenue, costs and profit.
options.B: We estimate profit using some records.
options.C: We mainly judge profit by the money remaining.
options.D: We do not know whether the business is profitable.

questions.text: How do you manage your business cash flow?

options.A: We forecast cash inflows and outflows and plan ahead.
options.B: We monitor cash regularly but rarely forecast it.
options.C: We check cash when payments are due.
options.D: We frequently struggle to understand or manage our cash position.

questions.text: How do you plan for major business expenses and financial obligations?

options.A: We budget and plan for them in advance.
options.B: We plan for some major expenses.
options.C: We usually respond when expenses arise.
options.D: We have no consistent financial planning process.

questions.text: How well do you understand your target customers?

options.A: We have clearly identified customer groups and understand their needs.
options.B: We understand our main customers but have limited information.
options.C: We mainly rely on our existing customer relationships.
options.D: We have not clearly identified our target customers.

questions.text: How do you attract new customers?

options.A: Through a consistent marketing and customer acquisition strategy.
options.B: Through several methods, but without a consistent plan.
options.C: Mainly through referrals and occasional promotion.
options.D: We do not have a clear way of attracting new customers.

questions.text: How consistently do you track sales performance?

options.A: We record and review sales regularly against targets.
options.B: We record most sales but rarely analyse performance.
options.C: We estimate sales from memory or incomplete records.
options.D: We do not systematically track sales.

questions.text: How do you respond to customer feedback and complaints?

options.A: We collect feedback, record complaints and act on the findings.
options.B: We respond to most complaints but do not track patterns.
options.C: We respond only when a problem becomes serious.
options.D: We have no consistent process for handling feedback.

questions.text: How clearly are your daily business activities organised?

options.A: We have documented processes and clear responsibilities.
options.B: Most activities are organised, but some processes are undocumented.
options.C: Activities depend largely on individual experience.
options.D: We frequently experience confusion about what needs to be done.

questions.text: How do you manage stock, materials or business resources?

options.A: We maintain accurate records and review stock regularly.
options.B: We keep records but sometimes experience discrepancies.
options.C: We estimate available stock or resources.
options.D: We do not have a consistent tracking system.

questions.text: How consistently do you maintain the quality of your products or services?

options.A: We use clear quality standards and check performance regularly.
options.B: We check quality but do not document the process consistently.
options.C: We mainly rely on customer complaints to identify problems.
options.D: We do not have a consistent quality-control process.

questions.text: How effectively does your business use technology or digital tools?

options.A: We use suitable tools to improve operations and decision-making.
options.B: We use some digital tools, but important processes remain manual.
options.C: We use technology mainly for basic communication.
options.D: We rarely use technology to support business operations.

questions.text: Are responsibilities clearly defined for the people working in your business?

options.A: Yes, responsibilities and reporting arrangements are clear.
options.B: Most responsibilities are clear, but some overlap.
options.C: Responsibilities are mainly communicated informally.
options.D: Responsibilities are unclear or frequently disputed.

questions.text: How do you monitor employee or team performance?

options.A: We use clear expectations and regular performance reviews.
options.B: We monitor performance informally and provide feedback.
options.C: We intervene mainly when problems occur.
options.D: We do not have a consistent way of monitoring performance.

questions.text: How do you identify and address skills gaps in your business?

options.A: We regularly identify skills gaps and organise appropriate learning.
options.B: We address skills gaps when we notice them.
options.C: We provide training occasionally.
options.D: We do not have a clear approach to skills development.

questions.text: How well can your business operate when you, the owner, are unavailable?

options.A: The team can handle most operations using established processes.
options.B: Some activities continue, but important decisions depend on me.
options.C: Most activities slow down when I am unavailable.
options.D: The business largely stops operating without me.

questions.text: How do you identify and manage business risks?

options.A: We regularly identify risks and implement mitigation measures.
options.B: We recognise major risks but manage them informally.
options.C: We usually address risks after problems occur.
options.D: We do not systematically identify business risks.

questions.text: What happens when your business experiences an unexpected disruption?

options.A: We have a documented continuity or recovery plan.
options.B: We have informal arrangements for major disruptions.
options.C: We try to resolve disruptions as they occur.
options.D: We have no clear approach to business disruptions.

questions.text: How prepared is your business to grow?

options.A: We have a realistic growth plan supported by resources and targets.
options.B: We have identified growth opportunities but need stronger planning.
options.C: We want to grow but have not identified clear steps.
options.D: We have not assessed our readiness for growth.

questions.text: How do you measure progress towards your business goals?

options.A: We track clear performance indicators and review them regularly.
options.B: We monitor some indicators but not consistently.
options.C: We mainly judge progress by general business activity.
options.D: We do not have a consistent way to measure progress.

AGRIFOOD360.name: AgriFood360 Free Business Health Assessment
AGRIFOOD360.audience: farms, agribusinesses, cooperatives and agricultural traders, processors and input/output market actors
dimensions: Storage, Post-Harvest Handling and Cold Chain
Market Access and Value Chain Position

questions.text: Do you keep records of planting dates, inputs used and yields each season?

options.A: Yes, detailed records for every season, used to plan input needs.
options.B: Yes, basic records, but not consistently reviewed.
options.C: We keep informal notes or rely on memory.
options.D: We do not keep any production records.

questions.text: How do you decide which crop varieties, breeds or farming methods to use?

options.A: Based on documented performance data, soil or agro-ecological testing and extension advice.
options.B: Based on some testing or advice, combined with past experience.
options.C: Mainly based on what neighbours or family have always used.
options.D: Without a consistent method; decisions change year to year.

questions.text: How do you manage soil fertility, pest and disease control on your farm or in your operation?

options.A: We follow a planned programme, such as soil testing, integrated pest management or certified inputs.
options.B: We apply inputs regularly but without a documented plan.
options.C: We react only when problems appear.
options.D: We have no regular soil, pest or disease management practice.

questions.text: How do you monitor and improve productivity (yield per acre, output per animal, or production efficiency) over time?

options.A: We track productivity each season and use it to adjust practices.
options.B: We have a general sense of whether productivity is improving.
options.C: We rarely compare productivity across seasons.
options.D: We do not track productivity at all.

questions.text: How exposed is your production to seasonal and climate-related disruption, such as erratic rainfall, drought or flooding?

options.A: We have specific measures, such as irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties or a diversified calendar, that substantially reduce this exposure.
options.B: We have some measures in place, but they only partly reduce exposure.
options.C: We are aware of the exposure but have taken little action.
options.D: Our production depends almost entirely on favourable weather, with no mitigation.

questions.text: Do you have access to reliable water for irrigation or livestock, independent of rainfall?

options.A: Yes, a reliable year-round water source and irrigation system.
options.B: Yes, but access is inconsistent or seasonal.
options.C: Limited access, mostly dependent on rain.
options.D: No reliable water access beyond rainfall.

questions.text: How do you plan your production calendar around seasonal risk, such as planting and harvest timing or off-season activities?

options.A: We actively plan and adjust the calendar each season based on forecasts and past experience.
options.B: We follow a general seasonal pattern with occasional adjustments.
options.C: We follow the same calendar every year regardless of conditions.
options.D: We have no deliberate seasonal planning.

questions.text: What would happen to your business if this season’s harvest or production failed significantly?

options.A: We have savings, insurance or alternative income that would absorb the loss.
options.B: We would be under pressure but could recover within a season or two.
options.C: It would set the business back significantly, with no clear recovery plan.
options.D: It would likely end the business or force us to stop operating.

questions.text: How reliably can you access the seeds, feed, fertiliser or other inputs you need, when you need them?

options.A: Reliable access through established, trusted suppliers, planned in advance.
options.B: Generally accessible but with occasional delays or shortages.
options.C: Frequently difficult to access on time.
options.D: Access is a persistent problem that regularly disrupts production.

questions.text: How do you finance the purchase of inputs each season?

options.A: Through planned working capital, savings or affordable credit secured in advance.
options.B: A mix of own funds and informal borrowing, arranged as the season approaches.
options.C: Mostly informal, high-cost borrowing or delayed purchases.
options.D: We often cannot afford the inputs we need.

questions.text: How confident are you in the quality of the inputs, such as seeds, feed or agrochemicals, that you currently use?

options.A: High confidence; inputs are from certified or verified sources.
options.B: Reasonably confident, though sources are not always verified.
options.C: Uncertain; we use whatever is available or affordable.
options.D: We have had repeated problems with poor-quality inputs.

questions.text: Do you have more than one reliable source for your most critical input?

options.A: Yes, at least two reliable alternative suppliers.
options.B: One main supplier, with an occasional backup.
options.C: Only one supplier, with no real alternative.
options.D: We do not have a consistent supplier at all.

questions.dimension: Storage, Post-Harvest Handling and Cold Chain
questions.text: What share of your harvest or production is typically lost between production and sale, due to spoilage, pests or poor handling?

options.A: Very low losses, under about 5 percent, with measures in place to keep it that way.
options.B: Moderate losses, roughly 5 to 15 percent.
options.C: Significant losses, roughly 15 to 30 percent.
options.D: High losses, over about 30 percent, with no real control over it.

questions.dimension: Storage, Post-Harvest Handling and Cold Chain
questions.text: What storage facilities do you use for your product between production and sale?

options.A: Proper, purpose-built storage, such as warehousing, cold storage or controlled-atmosphere storage, appropriate to the product.
options.B: Basic but adequate storage, with some protection from pests and moisture.
options.C: Informal or improvised storage with limited protection.
options.D: No dedicated storage; products are kept however is available.

questions.dimension: Storage, Post-Harvest Handling and Cold Chain
questions.text: If your product needs a cold chain to maintain quality, how reliable is it?

options.A: Reliable, consistent cold chain from production through to sale (or the product does not require one).
options.B: Partially reliable, with occasional breaks or gaps.
options.C: Frequently breaks down or is unavailable when needed.
options.D: No cold chain exists, even though the product needs one.

questions.dimension: Storage, Post-Harvest Handling and Cold Chain
questions.text: How do you handle grading, cleaning, packaging or basic processing before sale?

options.A: We consistently grade, clean and package to meet buyer or market standards.
options.B: We do this sometimes, depending on the buyer or market.
options.C: We do minimal grading or packaging, mostly selling as harvested.
options.D: We do not grade, clean or package our product at all.

questions.dimension: Market Access and Value Chain Position
questions.text: How do you currently sell your produce or products?

options.A: Through stable off-take agreements, contracts or established buyers at agreed prices.
options.B: Mainly to known traders or markets, without formal agreements.
options.C: Mostly at the farm gate, to whoever is available, at prevailing prices.
options.D: We regularly struggle to find a buyer at all.

questions.dimension: Market Access and Value Chain Position
questions.text: How well do you understand current prices and demand for your product before you sell?

options.A: We actively track prices and demand across more than one market or buyer.
options.B: We have a general sense of prices from one main source.
options.C: We mostly rely on what the first buyer offers.
options.D: We have little or no information on prices before selling.

questions.dimension: Market Access and Value Chain Position
questions.text: Where does your business sit in the value chain: raw production only, or also grading, processing, branding or direct sale?

options.A: We add meaningful value, such as processing, grading, branding or direct sale to end buyers, beyond raw production.
options.B: We do some basic value addition some of the time.
options.C: We sell raw, unprocessed product almost exclusively.
options.D: We have no involvement beyond production and no plan to add value.

questions.dimension: Market Access and Value Chain Position
questions.text: How dependent is your business on a single buyer or a single market?

options.A: We sell to several buyers or markets, so losing one would not seriously harm the business.
options.B: We have more than one buyer, but one accounts for most of our sales.
options.C: We depend almost entirely on a single buyer or market.
options.D: We have one buyer and no realistic alternative if that relationship ended.

questions.dimension: Market Access and Value Chain Position
questions.text: Are you part of, or do you have access to, a cooperative, farmer group, aggregator or association that strengthens your market position?

options.A: Yes, active membership that provides real benefits, such as bulk input or sale prices, market information or training.
options.B: Yes, membership exists, but we make limited use of it.
options.C: We know of such groups but are not part of one.
options.D: No such group is accessible to us.

questions.text: How do you record and track the income and costs of your agricultural business?

options.A: Consistent, season-by-season financial records covering all major costs and income.
options.B: Basic records that cover some, but not all, costs and income.
options.C: Informal tracking, mostly from memory.
options.D: We keep no financial records at all.

questions.text: Do you know your actual cost of production per unit, such as per bag, per acre, per animal or per batch?

options.A: Yes, calculated and used to set prices or decide what to produce.
options.B: We have a rough estimate, but it is not regularly updated.
options.C: We do not calculate this; we judge profitability by feel.
options.D: We have no idea what our production actually costs.

questions.text: How do you manage risks such as crop or livestock loss, price swings or input cost increases?

options.A: Through specific measures, such as insurance, diversification, contracts or reserves, matched to our main risks.
options.B: We are aware of the main risks but only manage some of them.
options.C: We deal with problems only as they happen, without a plan.
options.D: We have no way of managing these risks and absorb whatever happens.

questions.text: How ready is this agribusiness to grow, whether by expanding production, adding buyers, accessing larger finance or moving into new markets?

options.A: We have a clear growth plan and the records, systems or finance needed to pursue it.
options.B: We want to grow and have some of what is needed, but gaps remain.
options.C: We would like to grow but do not have a plan or the basics in place.
options.D: Growth is not something we have been able to consider; we are focused on surviving each season.

ESO360.name: ESO360 Free Business Health Assessment
ESO360.audience: enterprise support organisations: accelerators, incubators, mentorship programmes and business-development providers

questions.text: How is the content and structure of your programme (curriculum, milestones, support services) decided?

options.A: Based on documented needs assessments, evidence of what works, and regular curriculum review.
options.B: Based on some needs assessment or benchmarking, updated occasionally.
options.C: Mainly based on what previous cohorts or staff experience suggest.
options.D: We do not have a defined curriculum or programme structure.

questions.text: How well does your programme design match the stage and needs of the enterprises you support, such as pre-seed, early growth or scale-up?

options.A: Programme tracks are tailored to specific stages or needs, with clear entry and exit criteria.
options.B: Some differentiation by stage, but most support is generic.
options.C: One-size-fits-all programme regardless of enterprise stage.
options.D: We have not assessed whether our programme matches participants’ needs.

questions.text: How do you keep programme content and delivery methods current, based on market trends, new tools or participant feedback?

options.A: We review and update content systematically each cycle, using feedback and external input.
options.B: We make occasional updates when something clearly needs fixing.
options.C: Content has stayed largely the same for several cycles.
options.D: We have no process for reviewing or updating programme content.

questions.text: How clearly are the expected outcomes of your programme, for participants and for your organisation, defined and communicated?

options.A: Clear, specific outcomes are defined, documented and shared with participants and stakeholders.
options.B: General outcomes are understood internally but not clearly documented or communicated.
options.C: Outcomes are vague or differ depending on who you ask.
options.D: We have not defined what success looks like for this programme.

questions.text: How do you attract applicants for each cohort or intake?

options.A: Through a planned, multi-channel outreach strategy reaching beyond our existing network.
options.B: Mainly through our existing network and occasional targeted outreach.
options.C: Largely passive; we rely on word of mouth or inbound interest.
options.D: We struggle to attract enough applicants to fill a cohort.

questions.text: How do you select participants or enterprises to support?

options.A: Using documented, consistent selection criteria and a structured review process.
options.B: Using general criteria, but the process varies between cohorts or reviewers.
options.C: Mostly informal judgement calls with little documentation.
options.D: We accept most applicants with no real selection process.

questions.text: How well do you track and understand the diversity, such as gender, geography, sector or business stage, of your applicant pool and selected cohorts?

options.A: We track this systematically and use it to guide outreach and selection.
options.B: We have some data on this but do not act on it consistently.
options.C: We have a general impression but no real data.
options.D: We do not track this at all.

questions.text: How confident are you that the enterprises you select are a good fit for what your programme can actually deliver?

options.A: High confidence, supported by clear fit criteria applied consistently.
options.B: Reasonably confident, though mismatches happen occasionally.
options.C: Mismatches between participant needs and programme offer are common.
options.D: We have no way of assessing fit before selection.

questions.text: How do you recruit, vet and match mentors, coaches or advisors to participants?

options.A: A documented process for recruitment, vetting and matching based on participant needs.
options.B: Some process exists, but matching is often ad hoc.
options.C: We use whichever mentors are available, with little matching.
options.D: We do not have a structured mentor or advisor network.

questions.text: How do you monitor and support the quality of mentorship or advisory sessions actually delivered?

options.A: We track session delivery and quality, and act on participant or mentor feedback.
options.B: We get occasional feedback but do not systematically monitor quality.
options.C: We assume sessions happen but rarely verify quality or completion.
options.D: We have no visibility into whether mentorship sessions actually happen or help.

questions.text: Do you have enough qualified staff, facilitators, mentors or advisors to deliver your current programme commitments?

options.A: Yes, sufficient capacity with some ability to flex for growth.
options.B: Generally sufficient, but it is a regular stretch.
options.C: Frequently under-resourced, affecting delivery quality.
options.D: We consistently lack the people needed to deliver what we have promised.

questions.text: How do you build the skills and performance of your own facilitators, mentors and programme staff over time?

options.A: Through a deliberate development plan, such as training, feedback or performance review, for programme delivery staff.
options.B: Occasional training or feedback, but no consistent plan.
options.C: Staff mostly develop skills informally, on the job.
options.D: We have no process for developing programme delivery capacity.

questions.text: What data do you collect on participants during and after the programme, such as revenue, jobs, investment raised or survival?

options.A: We systematically collect defined outcome metrics during the programme and track them afterward.
options.B: We collect some data during the programme, but tracking after it ends is limited.
options.C: We collect anecdotal success stories, not structured data.
options.D: We do not collect outcome data on participants.

questions.text: How do you know whether your programme is actually achieving its intended outcomes?

options.A: We analyse outcome data against defined targets or a theory of change, regularly.
options.B: We review outcomes informally, without a clear benchmark.
options.C: We assume the programme works because participants complete it.
options.D: We have no way of knowing whether the programme achieves its outcomes.

questions.text: How do you use monitoring and evaluation findings to improve the programme?

options.A: Findings directly inform changes to curriculum, selection or delivery each cycle.
options.B: Findings are reviewed but changes happen only occasionally.
options.C: Findings are collected but rarely acted on.
options.D: We do not generate findings that could inform improvement.

questions.text: How do you maintain contact with and track alumni after they exit the programme?

options.A: Structured alumni engagement and tracking, with defined check-in points.
options.B: Some informal contact with alumni, but not systematic.
options.C: Contact with alumni mostly ends once the programme is over.
options.D: We lose touch with almost all participants after exit.

questions.text: How diversified are your organisation’s funding sources, such as donors, fees, corporate partners, government or earned revenue?

options.A: Multiple diversified sources, with no single source representing most of our funding.
options.B: A few sources, but one or two account for most of our funding.
options.C: Heavily dependent on a single donor or funding source.
options.D: We have no secured funding beyond the current cycle.

questions.text: How far in advance is your funding or revenue secured relative to your programme delivery commitments?

options.A: Funding is secured well beyond the current cycle, supporting multi-year planning.
options.B: Funding covers the current cycle, with some visibility beyond it.
options.C: Funding is usually secured only just in time for the current cycle.
options.D: We frequently deliver programmes without confirmed funding in place.

questions.text: Do you have a plan or model for how your organisation sustains itself, or becomes self-sustaining, beyond grant funding?

options.A: Yes, a documented plan with a credible path toward diversified or earned revenue.
options.B: We have ideas about sustainability but no documented plan.
options.C: We rely entirely on securing the next grant, with no sustainability plan.
options.D: We have not considered how the organisation sustains itself long term.

questions.text: How do you build and manage relationships with partner organisations, such as investors, corporates, government or other ESOs?

options.A: Deliberate partnership strategy with defined roles, managed relationships and mutual value.
options.B: Several partnerships exist, but they are managed informally.
options.C: Partnerships are occasional and largely reactive.
options.D: We have few or no active partnerships.

questions.text: How do you report your results and impact to funders, partners and the public?

options.A: Clear, evidence-based reporting aligned to agreed indicators, on a regular schedule.
options.B: We report when required, using whatever data is readily available.
options.C: Reporting is inconsistent and often reconstructed after the fact.
options.D: We have no regular reporting process.

questions.text: Does your organisation have a documented strategy or business plan guiding its own direction?

options.A: Yes, a current strategy with clear priorities, reviewed regularly.
options.B: Yes, but it is outdated or rarely referenced.
options.C: We have general direction but nothing documented.
options.D: We have no strategic plan for the organisation itself.

questions.text: How are governance and oversight of your organisation structured, such as a board, advisory committee or management team?

options.A: Active governance body with clear oversight, meeting regularly and holding management accountable.
options.B: A governance body exists but meets infrequently or has limited influence.
options.C: Governance exists mostly on paper.
options.D: We have no formal governance structure.

questions.text: How well can your organisation continue operating if a key staff member, such as the director, were unavailable?

options.A: Documented systems, succession plans and shared knowledge mean the organisation would continue smoothly.
options.B: Some continuity exists, but key knowledge sits with one or two people.
options.C: Most critical functions would stall without that person.
options.D: The organisation would likely stop functioning without that person.

questions.text: How do you identify and manage organisational risks, such as financial, reputational, compliance or staff-turnover risks?

options.A: Through a documented risk management approach reviewed regularly.
options.B: We recognise major risks but manage them informally.
options.C: We deal with risks only as they arise.
options.D: We have no process for identifying or managing organisational risks.
